ch06.title: Zoroaster
ch06.summary: The Iranian prophet who reduced the old pantheon to one Wise Lord, Ahura Mazda, and recast existence as a moral war of truth against the Lie: the Gathas and the Avesta, the cosmic dualism, fire and the Towers of Silence, and the fiercely debated inheritance the West may owe it — the devil, angels, heaven and hell, judgment, resurrection, and the apocalypse.

ch06.plateCaption: The sacred fire held in its vessel (ātash), the living centre of Zoroastrian worship. An original rendering, not a specific fire-holder.

ch07.title: Pre-exilic Israel
ch07.summary: How a people became monotheist: the historical religion of Iron Age Israel and Judah before the exile, reconstructed from archaeology and inscriptions — Israel's emergence within Canaan, Yahweh merged with El and paired with Asherah, the folk religion of high places and figurines, the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah, and the long road from many gods to one.
ch07.plateCaption: The seven-branched lampstand (menorah) described in Exodus. An original line drawing after the textual description — not a depiction of a specific object.

ch08.title: Early Greece
ch08.summary: The gods before the philosophers: Zeus and the Olympians already named on Bronze Age Linear B tablets, a religion with no scripture but with Homer and Hesiod as its canon, the succession myth borrowed from the Near East, sacrifice and oracles and the grim house of Hades — and the mystery cults of Eleusis and Orpheus that first promised the soul something better.
ch08.plateCaption: The lyre, instrument of the poets, over a Greek-key frieze. An original rendering of the forms, not a copy of a painted vase.

game.title: Divine Casualties — War of the Gods

ch09.title: Early China
ch09.summary: Ancestors, oracle bones, and the Mandate of Heaven: the Shang kings divining by fire-cracked bone to the high god Di and the royal dead, the ritual bronzes cast to feed the ancestors, and the Zhou revolution that made Heaven a moral judge who grants and revokes the right to rule — the religion in which Chinese writing itself was born.
ch09.plateCaption: A Shang–Zhou ritual bronze (ding), with a suggestion of the taotie band. An original rendering, not a specific excavated vessel.

ch58.title: Canaanite & Phoenician
ch58.summary: The gods the Bible fought — recovered from their own words at Ugarit. The pantheon of El the aged father-god, Asherah, and Baal the storm-god, and the Baal Cycle (Baal defeats the Sea, is swallowed by Death, and returns); the decisive fact that Israelite religion grew up within Canaanite religion (Yahweh inheriting El’s titles and Baal’s cloud-riding imagery, Asherah as his consort); the Phoenician city-gods (Melqart of Tyre, Eshmun of Sidon, Astarte) and Carthage’s Baal Hammon and Tanit; the tophet and the genuinely unsettled child-sacrifice debate; and the Phoenician gift of the alphabet, ancestor of all Western scripts. A symbology of the standing stone (massebah/Bethel), the Asherah pole, the sign of Tanit, and the letters born from pictures.

v54.title: The Behistun Inscription
v54.held: In place: Mount Bisotun, Kermanshah Province, Iran (UNESCO World Heritage Site)
v54.summary: Darius the Great's account of how he seized the Persian throne, carved about 60 metres up a cliff in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, beneath a relief of the king and the winged symbol of Ahuramazda. Copied at great risk by Henry Rawlinson, it opened cuneiform to modern reading.

v35.title: The Cyrus Cylinder
v35.summary: A clay barrel inscribed in Babylonian cuneiform after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon. It praises Cyrus as Marduk's chosen king and records the return of gods and peoples to their homes. It is often called the first charter of human rights, which it is not, and it is read beside the Bible's decree of Cyrus.

v07.title: The Ark of the Covenant
v07.held: No verified object; the Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds it is kept at Aksum
v07.summary: The most precisely described object in the Bible, measured to the half-cubit, and one found nowhere. What the texts say it was and did, the four traditions of its fate (Babylon, Mount Nebo, beneath the Temple, Aksum), and what archaeology can and cannot add.

v22.title: The Mesha Stele
v22.summary: A Moabite king's victory stone, smashed by fire and cold water in 1869 and rebuilt from a paper squeeze. It tells the story of 2 Kings 3 from the other side and carries the earliest certain mention of YHWH outside the Bible.

v23.title: The Tel Dan Stele
v23.summary: Three basalt fragments of an Aramaean king's boast, dug up in 1993–94, naming a king of Israel and bytdwd, the 'House of David'. The first mention of David outside the Bible, what it proves and what it doesn't.

v12.title: The Ketef Hinnom Silver Scrolls
v12.summary: Two tiny silver amulets from a Jerusalem tomb, excavated in 1979 and unrolled over three years, carrying the Priestly Blessing (‘May YHWH bless you and keep you’). They are about four centuries older than the Dead Sea Scrolls and the oldest known artefacts bearing words also found in the Bible.

v43.title: The Merneptah Stele
v43.summary: A pharaoh's granite hymn of victory, found by Flinders Petrie in 1896. Of its 28 lines, one names Israel, about 3,200 years ago, the earliest certain mention of Israel anywhere. The hieroglyphs say something precise about what Israel was.

v48.title: The Great Isaiah Scroll
v48.dated: c. 150–100 BCE (palaeography); radiocarbon ranges into the 4th–2nd centuries BCE
v48.held: The Israel Museum, Jerusalem (Shrine of the Book), 1QIsaᵃ
v48.summary: The only complete book of the Hebrew Bible among the Dead Sea Scrolls: all 66 chapters of Isaiah in 54 columns on a scroll 7.34 metres long, copied about a thousand years before the oldest complete medieval Hebrew Bibles, and remarkably close to them.

v56.title: The Phaistos Disc
v56.dated: Usually c. 1850–1600 BCE (Middle Minoan); the dating and even its authenticity have been questioned
v56.summary: A fired clay disc about 16 cm across, found in the Minoan palace of Phaistos in 1908, with 45 different signs pressed into it by stamps in a spiral on both sides: printing, in a sense, three thousand years early. It is unread, and probably unreadable unless more text turns up.

v39.title: The Derveni Papyrus
v39.dated: Roll c. 340–320 BCE; the text composed c. 400 BCE
v39.summary: A papyrus roll half-burned on a funeral pyre near Thessaloniki, the oldest surviving book in Europe. It is a philosopher's allegorical commentary on a secret Orphic poem about the birth of the gods, which opens by telling the uninitiated to shut the doors.

v55.title: The Oracle Bones of Anyang
v55.held: Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica (Taipei); Institute of Archaeology and museums in China; collections worldwide
v55.summary: Turtle shells and cattle shoulder-blades that Shang kings had cracked in fire to put questions to their ancestors, then had the questions and answers carved beside the cracks. Sold as 'dragon bones' for medicine until 1899, they are the oldest body of Chinese writing.

v81.title: The Mawangdui Silk Texts
v81.dated: Buried in Tomb 3, Mawangdui, in 168 BCE; excavated 1973
v81.summary: Silk manuscripts from a Han tomb, including two copies of the Laozi (Daodejing), then the oldest known. They put the De section before the Dao section and write heng, 'constant', where later editions avoid an emperor's name with chang.

adam.name: Adam
adam.desc: Formed from the dust of the ground and placed in the garden of Eden (Genesis 2), then sent out to till the soil. In the Qur'an, Ādam is the first prophet.

eve.name: Eve
eve.desc: The first woman, who eats the forbidden fruit at the serpent's urging (Genesis 3). Genesis does not name the fruit; the apple comes from later Latin tradition.

enoch.name: Enoch
enoch.desc: Seventh from Adam, who 'walked with God; and he was not, for God took him' (Genesis 5:24). He became the seer of the Books of Enoch, and in later mysticism the angel Metatron.

noah.name: Noah
noah.desc: Saved with his family and the animals from the flood in Genesis 6–9; God's covenant with him is sealed by the rainbow. Nūḥ is a prophet in the Qur'an.
noah.contested: The story has close parallels in older Mesopotamian flood stories; see The Flood (ch01).
